Over the same period, there were 3 strong, 9 moderate, and 11 weak episodes. El Niño episodes typically emerge around May or June, strengthen through the third quarter of the year, peak near year-end, and dissipate during the first half of the following year. As a result, much of the associated rainfall anomaly occurs during the second half of the year, overlapping with the growing season for several major internationally traded commodities.

Episodes vary widely in intensity, and only a minority—eight out of 26 episodes since 1950—have been classified as strong or very strong.6 Commodity prices are higher during ENSO episodes than during neutral periods (box 1). However, price sensitivity differs from volatility transmission: a large movement in a commodity’s own price does not necessarily make it a stronger source of volatility for other markets. The results indicate that the strong phase of the 2015-16 El Niño was associated with much larger increases in transmitted connectedness than the weak phase (figure SF .4.B). Soybeans recorded the largest increase in connectedness during the strong phase, followed by maize. During the weak phase, maize transmission was broadly unchanged, while the increase for soybeans was similar to that for non-food commodities.

The agency also estimates an 83 percent chance that it will become the strongest El Niño since 1950 (when comparable records begin) during October–De- cember 2026 (figure 13.A).2 El Niño typically brings drier conditions to parts of Australia, Central America, the Sahel, South and Southeast Asia, and Southern Africa, and wetter conditions to parts of Central Asia, China, and the southern United States. Its effects on East Africa vary by location and season. Historically, the prices of food and beverage commodities have increased materially during El Niño episodes, as extreme weather conditions hinder production (figure 13.B). In the current episode, notable effects are expected in cocoa, palm oil, rice, and sugar markets, although annual average prices are forecast to increase significantly only for palm oil and rice.

Outlook The food price index is projected to rise by 10 percent in 2026, followed by a further increase of 7 percent in 2027, before retreating by 5 percent in 2028 as various supply pressures subside (table 1). Most commodity analysis appropriately focuses on the supply and demand fundamentals of individual markets. While that approach remains important, it provides only a partial view when volatility associated with one commodity is linked to developments in other commodity markets. This Special Focus examines price volatility connectedness across 15 internationally traded commodities in six groups—energy, food, industrial metals, livestock, precious metals, and soft commodities (such as coffee and cotton)— using daily data from 2006 to 2026. Price volatility connectedness measures how much of the variance in a commodity’s price volatility can be explained by shocks affecting prices in other commodity markets.

Commodity price fluctuations are highly consequential for economic conditions in many emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs). Moreover, individual commodity prices often move in tandem with other commodity prices, so determining the origin of price volatility can be challenging. Using a measure of price volatility connectedness across 15 internationally traded commodities over 2006–26, commodity-specific factors are found to dominate price volatility: roughly two-thirds is commodity-specific, while about one-third is associated with shocks in other commodity markets. About half of measured connectedness reflects links within broad commodity groups. Industrial metals and food are the principal net-transmitting groups, while livestock and soft commodities are the main net receivers.
